Great goal — body recomposition (losing fat while building muscle simultaneously) is definitely achievable, especially if you're newer to training or returning after a break. Here's how to approach it:
Training
Prioritize resistance training 3–5 days per week. Lifting is the primary driver of muscle growth, and it also burns calories and preserves muscle while in a deficit. Focus on progressive overload — gradually increasing weight, reps, or intensity over time. Compound movements (squats, deadlifts, bench, rows, overhead press) give you the most bang for your buck.
Add cardio as a tool, not the centerpiece. 2–3 sessions of moderate cardio per week supports fat loss without eating into recovery.
Nutrition
Protein is the most important dial to turn. Aim for roughly 0.7–1g of protein per pound of bodyweight daily. This preserves and builds muscle even in a slight caloric deficit.
Eat at a small caloric deficit (around 200–300 calories below maintenance). A large deficit speeds fat loss but sacrifices muscle — the sweet spot lets you do both. If you're a beginner, you may even be able to recomp at maintenance calories.
Don't fear carbs — they fuel your workouts and support performance. Time them around training if possible.
Recovery
Sleep is where muscle is actually built. Aim for 7–9 hours. Poor sleep tanks both fat loss (cortisol, hunger hormones) and muscle gain (growth hormone, protein synthesis).
Manage stress — elevated cortisol makes fat loss harder and muscle building slower.
Realistic expectations
Recomposition is slower than doing one or the other exclusively. If you optimize purely for fat loss or purely for muscle gain, you'll progress faster in that direction. Recomp is the right call when you want both, but patience is key — think months, not weeks.

Great question — post-workout nutrition is one of the highest-leverage recovery levers. Here's what the evidence points to:
What to eat
Protein is the priority. Aim for 20–40g of high-quality protein to kick off muscle protein synthesis. Good sources: chicken, eggs, Greek yogurt, cottage cheese, whey protein shake.
Carbohydrates help replenish glycogen and actually enhance protein uptake. Aim for roughly a 2:1 or 3:1 carb-to-protein ratio if your session was intense. Rice, oats, fruit, or potatoes all work well.
Don't fear fat — it slightly slows digestion but doesn't blunt the anabolic response meaningfully for most people. Just don't make it the focus.
When to eat it
The classic "anabolic window" (eat within 30 minutes or lose gains) is largely overstated. That said, eating within 1–2 hours post-workout is a solid practical target.
If you trained fasted or it's been 4+ hours since your last meal, sooner is better — closer to 30–60 minutes.
If you ate a solid pre-workout meal 1–2 hours before training, you have more flexibility.
Practical rule of thumb
A meal or shake with ~30–40g protein + some carbs within 1–2 hours covers you well for the vast majority of cases. Something like Greek yogurt with fruit, a chicken rice bowl, or a protein shake with a banana hits all the marks without overthinking it.
Total daily protein intake (around 0.7–1g per pound of bodyweight) matters more than any single post-workout meal, so don't stress if the timing isn't perfect every session.

Happy to help! A 2-month plateau is really common and usually comes down to one of a few culprits:
1. Progressive Overload Has Stalled Your body adapts to the same stimulus. If you've been lifting the same weights/reps for months, that's likely the core issue. Try:
Adding small weight increments (even 2.5 lb plates)
Adding 1 rep per set each week before bumping weight
Tracking every session so you can see when you last progressed
2. Not Eating Enough Strength gain requires adequate calories and protein. A rough target is 0.7–1g of protein per pound of bodyweight daily. If you're under-eating, no program will save you.
3. Program Needs Variation If you've been on the exact same routine for months, consider:
Swapping to a structured program (5/3/1, GZCLP, or Starting Strength are great for pure strength)
Changing rep ranges periodically (e.g., a week of heavier 3x3 work)
4. Recovery Issues Sleep is when strength is actually built. 7–9 hours matters more than most people realize. Stress and under-recovery can flatline progress even with a perfect program.
5. Technique Ceiling Sometimes a form breakdown is limiting how much you can actually lift. A video review of your main lifts (squat, bench, deadlift) can reveal easy wins.

The most common fix for someone stuck 2 months: switch to a structured linear progression program and make sure you're eating enough. Those two changes alone resolve most plateaus.
